item.title: Germany's far-right AfD says 'democracy demands' parties work with them after state election win
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cpd0113082eo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Germany's far-right AfD says 'democracy demands' parties work with them after state election win - Published The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is "very, very close" to taking power in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, its deputy parliamentary leader has told the BBC, after a historic victory in elections there. Sunday's preliminary results show it fell three seats short of an outright majority, with 43.8% of the vote. It is now seeking support from other parties or individuals in order to govern. While most German political parties refuse to work with the AfD, Beatrix von Storch called for its opponents to enter talks and said: "You cannot say, I do not accept the vote of the people". Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he was "deeply shocked" by the result, describing it as "seismic... not just in the country but also in my own political party and I take that very seriously". His party, the conservative CDU, saw its share of the vote almost halved to 17.2% in the state's preliminary results. Merz said it was not possible to return to "business as usual", adding that the country needed "profound reforms" and the CDU needed to "reach people at an emotional level". No far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing and local education. Von Storch said the state's results "were on the table and now democrats have to talk to [one] another. This is what democracy demands". She added that if parties refused to work with the AfD, "then we might end up in severe chaos and maybe we have a new election". Her comments were echoed by AfD's leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, who told a news conference on Monday that the party had won a "clear mandate to govern". The state's defeated premier, the CDU's Sven Schulze, also said the mandate to govern Saxony-Anhalt "now lies with the AfD". Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund, 35. The party's plans for Saxony-Anhalt, which include segregating child refugees into special classes and setting up a task-force to help detain and deport migrants who no longer have the right to be in the state, are highly controversial within Germany. The AfD is currently heading for 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament instead of the 42 needed for an outright majority, although the result has not yet been finalised. Von Storch told the BBC the AfD was talking to individuals within the CDU group - the largest party in both the state's outgoing coalition and Germany's government - because they were "very, very unhappy with their own party". What could happen now? One idea being floated is an informal deal whereby a small party - the BSW - could give their tacit support to allow the AfD to form a minority government. The left-wing populist BSW, which is set to win five seats, is also tough on immigration and backs importing Russian gas. Siegmund said discussions with other parties were initiated on Sunday night and could potentially take days or weeks to conclude. "We reach out to everybody first, we will have consultations and then we'll see whether [there are] individual parliamentary groups or MPs who would be willing to help us," he added. Another possibility - at least in theory - is a messy, minority coalition government led by the conservative CDU party. But that appears very unlikely. There's also the prospect of another election to break the deadlock - an idea which has been mooted by Siegmund who has said he doesn't want to compromise on his policy goals. The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states. They also won the 2024 state election in neighbouring Thuringia, but failed to secure enough seats to win power. Merz described the Saxony-Anhalt defeat as the worst the CDU had suffered "in years, if not decades", acknowledging that the results in upcoming regional elections in Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania and Berlin could have "increasing significance". Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally. Commentators and political opponents called AfD's victory a watershed and break with the past. "This isn't just about Saxony-Anhalt," Siegmund told supporters overnight. "It's a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal." On Sunday, US President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the state's projected results on his Truth Social platform. Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev then took a screengrab of Trump's post and praised a "historic win for the pragmatic AfD". Dmitriev had earlier praised the Russia-friendly AfD as "the party of hope and reason, co-operation truth and hope for Germany". Ahead of Germany's federal election last year, US Vice-President JD Vance endorsed the party, in a move criticised in Germany as political interference. Polish centre-right Prime Minister Donald Tusk saw the result very differently, saying "in Poland only idiots and traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD". Asked about those who had expressed fears over the far-right party gaining power in the state, deputy parliamentary leader Beatrix von Storch told the BBC that its supporters were afraid of "losing our economy, they are afraid of losing our inner security". She said conservative voters were turning to alternative political parties because they were not being listened to. She added that the party's detractors should: "Wake up and realise what happened in several other European states... The conservative parties will disappear from the landscape as it happened in Italy, as it's about to happen in the UK, as it might also happen in France". - Published12 hours ago - Published16 hours ago - Published2 days ago

item.title: Thousands turn out in Serbia for funeral of 'Butcher of Bosnia' Ratko Mladić
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn5dkk7yw74o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Thousands turn out in Serbia for funeral of 'Butcher of Bosnia' Ratko Mladić - Published Thousands of people have turned out in Serbia's capital, Belgrade, to attend the funeral of the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić. Widely known as the Butcher of Bosnia, Mladić died at the age of 84 while serving a life sentence in the UN prison in The Hague, the Netherlands. He was found guilty of genocide by a UN war crimes tribunal for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when around 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed. It was described as Europe's worst atrocity since World War Two. A Serbian government minister had initially said that Mladić would be given a state funeral but those plans were changed after objections from some European leaders. On Monday, the EU denounced Mladić's "glorification". "Ratko Mladić was a convicted war criminal who had committed war crimes, genocide, and crimes against humanity," the EU said in a statement. "Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries," the statement said. Serbia has been a candidate to join the EU since 2012, even though membership talks have recently stalled. Ratko Mladić commanded Bosnian Serb forces in the 1990s against the Bosnian Croat and Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim) armies. During the 1992-1995 Bosnian war, his troops committed what became known as "ethnic cleansing" in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a bid to expel the non-Serbian population by force. They besieged the capital city of Sarajevo, with the deaths of more than 10,000 people. Mladić was arrested in 2011, 16 years after he was first indicted, and sentenced to life in prison in 2021 after a nine-year trial. Despite his conviction for genocide, Mladić remains a national figure perceived by many Serbs as a heroic defender of the nation. Many Serb nationalists see him as a hero and protector, particularly in the Bosnian Serb entity of Republika Srpska, where his death sparked vigils. Several Serbian government ministers joined the crowds paying tribute outside the church where Mladić lay in state before the burial, including the Defence Minister Bratislav Gašić, and the Minister of Justice Nenad Vujić, local media reported. The funeral service was led by the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Porfirije, who said Mladić's name would remain "deeply etched in the memory and prayers of the majority of our Serbian Orthodox people, who feel and nurture a deep sense of gratitude towards him". Early in the day, long queues formed outside the small St Luka church, as people waited to go in and pay their respects to the coffin. Many of those in the crowds were army veterans and some men were draped in flags printed with his picture on. Crowds arrived several hours before the funeral began to light candles outside the church, accompanied by a choir on a loudspeaker in the sunshine. Inside the church, Mladić's coffin was guarded by several men, mainly war veterans, while his wife, son, and grandchildren stood inside receiving condolences. In a sign of the reverence held for the former general, his coffin was flown back to Serbia last week on a government plane, and was carried from the plane by six soldiers and draped in flags. Free bus services were organised from Bosnia and most towns in Serbia for anyone who wanted to pay their respects. On Sunday night, fans of the Serbian football club Red Star Belgrade unveiled a display of Mladic before their derby win over Partizan Belgrade. For others, the funeral has rekindled painful memories of the war. A woman in Sarajevo called Zdravka Gvozdjar - whose nine-year-old son was killed by Mladić-led forces during the siege of the city - told Reuters news agency it was "really horrible" that the funeral was taking place in Belgrade. Mladić "deserved to be erased from memory for good, not to be... promoted as a hero," she said. "He should be remembered only as a butcher." Thousands attended the funeral because he "remains a figure of national pride and defiance," said Daniella Peled, Editor at the Institute of War and Peace Reporting NGO - who covered Mladić's war crimes trial in detail. The war crimes tribunal "provided an incredibly detailed historical record of Mladić's crimes," she told the BBC, but the Serbian media and education system "has not reflected the true scale of his crimes or the perspectives of victims and survivors." Pro-government Serbian media "depict him as a loyal soldier who simply carried out his duties," Peled said. "It's extremely challenging for post-conflict societies to undertake a national reckoning or acknowledge responsibility for the crimes of the past." item.title: Israeli strikes in southern Lebanese village kill 12
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yl96vz0edo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Israeli strikes in southern Lebanese village kill 12 - Published Israeli air strikes on a village in southern Lebanon have killed at least 12 people, the Lebanese health ministry says. Eleven people, including two children and four women, were killed in a strike that destroyed a residential building in Kfar Roummane overnight. A second strike on a vehicle killed a paramedic. The Israeli military said it struck infrastructure sites belonging to the Shia Muslim armed group Hezbollah, as well as "several terrorists" transferring weapons, in retaliation for a drone attack on troops in an occupied area of the country. Israeli attacks across southern Lebanon have killed at least 27 people over the past three days, according to the health ministry. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said the "dangerous escalation" was jeopardising June's US-brokered ceasefire, which was meant to end the conflict between Israel and Hezbollah. He urged the international community to put pressure on Israel to stop the attacks. - Three farmers detained by Israel in Lebanon, village leader says - Published4 days ago - Eleven killed in Israeli strikes on southern Lebanon, authorities say - Published15 August The Israeli military has intensified its strikes in southern Lebanon in recent days. They have happened in places near the strip of territory that is occupied by Israeli troops, and large numbers of residents have again been fleeing those areas. The latest attacks targeted Kfar Roummane, in Nabatieh district, which is only a few hundred metres from what the Israeli military calls its "security zone". The first air strike destroyed a three-storey residential building near the town's Shuyuiya roundabout shortly after midnight, Lebanon's state-run National News Agency reported. The Lebanese health ministry said that in addition to the 11 people killed, eight were injured, including three children and a paramedic from the Islamic Health Association, which is an emergency service linked to Hezbollah. The second strike hit a vehicle carrying paramedics from the Islamic Risala Scout Association, killing one of them and injuring two others, according to the ministry. The Risala Scouts is an emergency service affiliated with the Amal movement, a Shia group allied to Hezbollah. The health ministry said the death toll "serves as further irrefutable evidence of the grave violations of international humanitarian law committed by the Israeli occupation, targeting medics and children". A resident of Kfar Roummane, Sara Moallaem, 35, told the BBC that she had been asleep with her five children in their rental home when she heard the explosions. She immediately grabbed her children and moved them into the home's "safe room" while they waited for the booms and the sirens to stop. Some of those killed in the strikes were distant relatives of Sara's husband. She insisted they were civilians with no affiliation to Hezbollah. Sara said she was planning to move her family to the coastal city of Sidon for their safety. "During the day, it is almost normal, [with] people going back and forth. But as it comes near the night, things escalate, and now my children are afraid and I am packing now for the sixth or seventh time. It is terrible," she explained. "Now that they are targeting civilians, I don't want to weep for my children." The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it struck "several Hezbollah terrorist infrastructure sites across southern Lebanon" overnight after the group's fighters launched two explosive drones towards Israeli troops operating in the Ali al-Taher ridge area, which is just south of Kfar Roummane and inside the Israeli-declared "security zone". "Additionally, the IDF struck several terrorists who were identified transferring weapons in the area of Kfar Roummane, in order to remove the threat they posed to IDF soldiers." "The claim that several uninvolved individuals were harmed as a result of the strikes is being reviewed," it added. The IDF also said it had struck the Nabatieh area and killed several Hezbollah fighters on Sunday following a separate drone attack. Lebanon's health ministry said 11 people were killed in Israeli strikes across the south of the country on Sunday. They included nine people in Nabatieh al-Fawqa, which is south of Kfar Roummane, and two women in Arab Salim, to the north of the village. There was no immediate comment from Hezbollah. But on Sunday, one of the group's members of parliament, Ali Ammar, declared that "the language of resistance is the only language that is effective against the Israeli enemy". The ceasefire agreement between Lebanon, Israel and the US calls for Hezbollah to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw gradually from southern Lebanon, and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area. Hezbollah has rejected the framework, saying the provisions linking Israel's withdrawal to the group's disarmament cross "all red lines". Lebanon was drawn into the war between Israel, the US and Iran on 2 March, when Hezbollah - which is supported by Iran - launched rockets into Israel in retaliation for a strike that killed Iran's supreme leader. Israel responded by launching a bombing campaign across Lebanon and invading a significant part of the country's south. At least 4,362 people have been killed in Lebanon during the conflict, including 395 women and 259 children, according to the health ministry, whose figures do not differentiate between combatants and civilians. Israeli authorities say 40 Israeli soldiers and four civilians have been killed during the conflict. Additional reporting by Ghaith Solh

item.title: Investigators begin work on why cargo plane overran Miami runway
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0e3p1j7n3ro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Investigators begin work on why cargo plane overran Miami runway - Published Officials are investigating what caused an Amazon cargo plane to overshoot the runway after landing at Miami International Airport in a deadly incident on Sunday. Five people were killed and five others seriously injured when the plane, which was operated by 21 Air, crashed just before 14:00 (18:00 GMT). The plane, a Boeing 767-300, crossed a road beyond the runway and hit several vehicles on the ground. It is not yet clear whether those who died were in the aircraft, on the ground, or both. Members of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), the federal agency investigating the incident, are at the site and will brief reporters on Monday afternoon. 21 Air, a charter company based in North Carolina, said it was "devastated by the accident involving one of our aircraft in Miami". Both 21 Air and Amazon said they were co-operating with the investigation. "At least five people have lost their lives, and five others are injured," Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said at a news conference on Sunday evening. She added that rescue crews arrived at the scene within "seconds" of the crash. Three of the five people injured were in critical condition, Miami Fire Chief Raied Jadallah said. Several of the injured were trapped inside or under vehicles on the ground, and needed to be extricated by fire and rescue crews, Jadallah added. Over 200 firefighters responded after the plane burst into flames. Experts who spoke to the Associated Press news agency said video footage of the plane's landing would present investigators with the question of whether or not the aircraft touched down within its designated zone on the runway - and if so, what happened. All flights at the airport were temporarily grounded by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The incident came over Labor Day weekend, one of the busiest travel times of the year. Locals have described the aftermath of the incident. Grace Mercado told CBS News she was in a vehicle nearby when she saw the aftermath. "The plane was up in smoke," she said. "It was just, it was like something from a movie. It was crazy." Beth Tilman told the New York Times she had seen a black cloud where the plane had crashed, and had smelled an acrid stench. "It wasn't trees burning. It wasn't mangroves burning. It was some other odour that I, honestly, had never smelled before," she said. Flight data from tracking site FlightRadar24 shows that the Amazon cargo flight was travelling at 112 knots (129mph, 207km/h) as it exited the "useable runway". In a blog post, the site said the plane came to rest near a car park that serves an Amazon warehouse and other businesses. There were light thunderstorms and gusting winds in Miami at the time of the incident, the site says. Kelly Nantel, Amazon's Director of Corporate Global Media Relations, said: "We're heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today's incident at Miami International Airport. "Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss. "The airplane, which was operated by 21 Air, was attempting to land when this incident occurred. We're working closely with local authorities and officials to learn more and will co-operate fully with any investigation." The statement from 21 Air's CEO Keith Winters said: "Our deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives. "Our immediate priorities are supporting those affected, assisting the authorities, and ensuring that accurate information is communicated as it becomes available." The plane had earlier departed Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The crash comes during one of the busiest travel weekends of the year in the US. Passengers at the airport told the BBC they were frustrated by the lack of information coming from officials, with many flights cancelled or delayed as a result of the incident. There were long queues at airline counters as people tried to reschedule travel plans, with some saying they would be forced to stay in Miami an extra night. "The earliest I could find to fly to San Francisco was Tuesday morning," said one traveller named Faroush. "I'll probably have to find a hotel and spend more time in Miami." The Transportation Safety Administration (TSA) said there would be 17 million travellers passing through US airports in the week leading up to Monday's Labor Day holiday. The TSA, which screens passengers flying in the US, predicted that 2.3 million people would fly on Sunday alone. Miami International Airport (MIA) is located near downtown Miami, and is one of the busiest airports in the country. "Founded in 1928, MIA is America's busiest airport for international freight and second busiest for international passengers, offers more flights to Latin America and the Caribbean than any other US airport," according to its website. About 60% of all international visitors to Florida arrive at this airport, it says. Did you witness the incident? Get in touch by clicking this link or use the form below. item.title: Grindr to pay £26m to settle claims it allegedly shared users' HIV status
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn8e63qdqwzo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Grindr to pay £26m to settle claims it allegedly shared users' HIV status - Published Grindr has agreed to pay £26m to settle a lawsuit over allegations it shared users' personal information - including their HIV status - with third parties. The world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app was sued in the High Court in 2024 over claims it misused people's personal information. The class action suit was later served in the US, with the law firm leading the case saying it had signed up more than 11,000 claimants. According to a US regulatory filing, Grindr will make two £13m payments to settle the claims. The firm said the settlement includes no admission of liability. Grindr stressed the claims relate to "historical data practices" before 2020 when it was owned by Chinese firm Kunlun. The filing submitted to the US Securities and Exchange Commission, external by Grindr said a settlement had been reached on 2 September. "While Grindr disputes the allegations, it recognizes and acknowledges the distress and loss of trust expressed by some of its UK users regarding that pre-2020 period," the company said in its filing. The firm has agreed to pay £13m to the counterparties by 31 December and a further £13m by 31 March 2027. 'Significant distress' The claims brought more than two years ago by law firm Austen Hayes alleged Grindr had shared sensitive data with third parties for commercial purposes, breaching UK privacy laws. It said this included information about the ethnicity and sexual orientation of its users. People on Grindr have the option to share their HIV status along with when they were last tested - a move it says aims to reduce stigma, facilitate conversations and help users make informed health choices. Chaya Hanoomanjee, the lawyer who led the claim, said in April 2024 claimants had "experienced significant distress" over their sensitive and private information being shared without their consent. She said the company "owes it to the LGBTQ+ community it serves to compensate those whose data has been compromised". Two data analytics services, Apptimize and Localytics, were identified as third parties with access to the sensitive data. The claim said a potentially unlimited number of third parties used it to customise advertisements to Grindr's users. It followed revelations in 2018 that Grindr had been sharing personal data, including the HIV status of its users, with the two data analytics providers. Grindr defended the practice at the time as in line with industry standards – but it said it then stopped sharing HIV data with those companies. It was fined £5.5m by Norway's data protection watchdog and, later in 2022, reprimanded by the UK Information Commissioner's Office for its data practices. The company said in its filing on Friday that since 2020, it had "overhauled" its privacy practices to help meet the "unique needs of its community". "Grindr is and remains a safe space for users, committed to transparency, user control, and responsible data practices," it said. item.title: Nepal observes national day of mourning for victims of flash flood disaster
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c2kw1qek7gdo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Nepal observes national day of mourning for victims of flash flood disaster - Published Nepalis observed a national day of mourning for the victims of the flash flood on Monday, lighting candles to mark the last day of the traditional 13-day Hindu mourning period. While flags were flown at half mast, commemorations were scaled back as rescue teams continue to search for survivors. Candlelight vigils were planned for Monday evening. At least 1,287 people are known to have died after a flash flood, believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse, swept through villages in a Himalayan valley along the border between Nepal and Tibet. Almost two weeks later, more than 5,000 people are still missing. Phanindra Paudel of the National Emergency Operation Centre (NEOC) told the Reuters news agency that there would be "no government programmes organised as the rescue and search operation is still going on in the flood-hit areas." Nepal's president, Ram Chandra Paudel, toured areas devastated by the floods on Monday, an aide told Reuters. The home ministry said that government offices, as well as missions abroad, would fly the national flag at half mast to mark the final day of the mourning period. Army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told Agence France-Presse that rescue efforts were continuing "with the same tempo we had on day one". "Our focus is on search and rescue at three levels - on ground, by air, and in the tunnels," he said. "We are making sure that no one is still stranded." Among the few places where rescuers still see a chance of finding survivors is in tunnels that form part of the region's hydropower stations, with hundreds of workers among the missing. Australian tunnel rescue expert Arnold Dix, who is advising Nepali teams, said in an update on X that the operation meant facing "multiple potential rescues, unfolding at the same time, in different places, each with its own dangers, uncertainties and lives that may still be saved." Four people have been rescued in recent days, three at hydropower stations or tunnels. On Saturday, a 64-year-old Nepali woman was pulled from her buried house on Saturday, more than 10 days after a wall of ice, rock and mud partially buried her house in the Nuwakot district. She was discovered alive on the fourth floor of the building by Nepal's Armed Police Force and airlifted to a hospital in Kathmandu for treatment. On Sunday rescue workers in China recovered twelve bodies in the Nepal-Tibet border, using excavators, shovels and ground penetrating radar at the site. At least 5,083 people are still missing in Nepal. On the Tibetan side, the death toll reported by Chinese media on Friday was 31, with 531 people unaccounted for. - Published3 days ago

item.title: New videos of man in 9/11 lawsuit reveal extremist links
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr4vn1e207go?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
New videos of man in 9/11 lawsuit reveal extremist links - Published The man at the heart of a $1 trillion (£733bn) lawsuit brought by 9/11 families had extensive links to Saudi government officials and went paintballing with one of al-Qaeda's future leaders, video obtained by the BBC reveals. The footage, which the FBI had within days of the 2001 attacks, stands in stark contrast to Omar al-Bayoumi's 25 years of denials that he was an extremist and a Saudi spy. Bayoumi, who claimed to be a student when he was in the United States, is seen in one clip embracing Anwar al-Awlaki, who would go on to lead al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula. In another, Bayoumi and Awlaki are paintballing near San Diego with an official from Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Islamic Affairs. The videos form part of the 9/11 families' lawsuit against Saudi Arabia and have never been shown publicly before. The lawsuit argues Saudi Arabia was complicit in the attacks and that Bayoumi aided two of the 19 hijackers who flew planes into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon - with another crashing in Pennsylvania. Bayoumi was arrested in the UK by the Metropolitan Police days after the attacks and the videos were found among his possessions, along with other crucial evidence. This included a diagram of a plane with a flight descent equation written alongside. Multiple FBI agents received copies of the diagram, but it was never shared with the British interrogators, even though it had been couriered to the police station where Bayoumi was being held in custody. The diagram was also kept from some FBI agents investigating Bayoumi, as well as from the 9/11 Commission - the independent inquiry into the largest mass murder in US history, in which nearly 3,000 people were killed. Bayoumi was never prosecuted. He and the Saudi government did not respond to the BBC's requests for comment, but both have always denied any involvement in, or prior knowledge of, the attacks. The FBI declined to comment. After a judge ruled the lawsuit could go ahead in 2018, thousands of documents, as well as videos and photographs, have been released to the court and also declassified through an executive order made by former President Joe Biden. BBC Panorama and Radio 4 have examined these documents, and spoken to dozens of special agents and investigators, to trace the evidence the FBI gathered about Bayoumi and Saudi Arabia's alleged involvement in 9/11 - and to understand why it was never fully pursued over 25 years. Our investigation also found: - The plane diagram was sent to the FBI's New York office and was analysed, according to an FBI source. But a US Department of Justice (DOJ) official told the BBC he was never shown a proposal to prosecute Bayoumi based on the evidence, even though "we've convicted people for less" - FBI agents in San Diego, where Bayoumi had lived in the US, repeatedly requested copies of evidence but never received most of it - The San Diego and Los Angeles FBI offices were both blocked from interviewing Bayoumi's Saudi government contacts - Staff on the 9/11 Commission objected to the conclusion that Bayoumi was "unlikely" to have been involved with extremists, prompting the report to attribute this to "our investigators who have dealt directly with him" Paintballing to 'train for jihad' Omar al-Bayoumi arrived in San Diego from Saudi Arabia in 1994. He claimed to be studying English, but court records show that within a few years he had, in effect, abandoned his studies. He was more usually found organising religious events, often with a camcorder pressed to his eye. One video Bayoumi filmed, from 1997 or early 1998, shows men, including Anwar al-Awlaki, paintballing. Filmed near San Diego, the group engages in urban combat scenes and target practice, many wearing military fatigues. At one point, some of the men charge into battle, shouting "Allahu Akbar". A visiting Saudi sheikh is with the group and Bayoumi can also be heard addressing Anwar al-Awlaki with the honorific "Sheikh Anwar". Paintballing emerged as a subject of interest in the FBI's post-9/11 counter-terrorism investigations, and the DOJ used paintball evidence in a number of terrorism prosecutions. Omar al-Bayoumi and Anwar al-Awlaki were involved in paintball sessions in San Diego for at least three years in the late 1990s and very early 2000s. When the FBI investigated after 9/11, agents were told some of the participants were taking part to train for jihad. Though Awlaki's extremist preaching would come into sharper focus after 9/11, at the time the paintballing video was recorded he already had connections to al-Qaeda operatives and was shortly to be investigated by the FBI. He was killed in a CIA drone strike in 2011. Panorama - 9/11: The Saudi Connection Watch on iPlayer now or on BBC One at 20:00 BST on Monday 7 September. You can also listen on BBC Sounds to the Radio 4 podcast Intrigue: A 9/11 Story. Saudi Arabia has stated that the paintball video does not reveal who "made" or "took" it. When he was questioned remotely in the 9/11 families' lawsuit in 2021, Bayoumi insisted he had not met Awlaki. The video evidence contradicting his claim was only made available, confidentially, to the court a year later - and placed on the public docket on 4 September this year. Another previously unreported clip shows Bayoumi embracing Awlaki in January 1998. Further footage records Bayoumi's many meetings with officials and preachers from Riyadh's Ministry of Islamic Affairs. He appears in a video with two ministry officials, one wielding a clipboard, at SeaWorld. Bayoumi passes the camera to his son and bounds into shot to record his presence with them. The Ministry of Islamic Affairs, created in 1993, was seen as dominated by clerics who espoused a radical view of Sunni Islam and exported it around the world. It spent hundreds of millions of dollars worldwide building mosques, and sent dozens of officials to the US, some of whom oversaw a network of preachers with hard-line views. Plane diagram found in Birmingham After the 9/11 attacks, Omar al-Bayoumi emerged as an early suspect in the FBI's investigation. His name had been found on an apartment rental agreement signed by the first two hijackers to arrive in the United States, Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar, who were part of a five man hijacking team that crashed a plane into the Pentagon. The FBI traced Bayoumi to Birmingham, UK, where he had moved with his family before 9/11. On 21 September 2001, officers from the Met Police's Anti-Terror Branch Special Operations team arrested Bayoumi at one of his properties. He was blue-lighted down to Paddington Green Police Station in London, where detectives began questioning him. Under UK law at the time, officers could only hold him for seven days without charge. The following morning, in Birmingham, officers began the meticulous process of logging and bagging up evidence in his properties - a cache of many thousands of pages of documents, hundreds of photographs, flight ticket stubs, phone cards, and carrier bags and boxes containing at least 80 videotapes. Within hours of the search starting, several items of documentary evidence - categorised as the highest priority at the direction of the FBI - were taken by police directly to Paddington Green, where the FBI had stationed an agent. This evidence included a phone book containing more than two dozen names of Saudi government officials in the US and Saudi Arabia; flight simulator software; tickets and travel documents; and the yellow lined page of a notebook with the sketch of a plane, which an officer had marked: "contains handwritten notes mathematical calculations re height of planes". Eighteen years later, the FBI would hand the notebook page to the court in the 9/11 families' lawsuit, following a subpoena. The page was made public in 2022. "It's the mathematical calculation of the crash," Jodi Westbrook Flowers, a member of the 9/11 families' legal team, told the BBC. "When we figured out what it was, we knew that it was the smoking gun that we'd been looking for." The equation, written in Omar al-Bayoumi's handwriting, indicates the height and distance required for a pilot to guide an aeroplane to a given object on the ground. Underneath it is a small drawing of a plane and a series of numbers. Last year, the federal judge in the families' lawsuit found the notebook page, on the face of it, "connects Bayoumi with knowledge of the 9/11 Attacks". In 2021, when questioned about it in court, Bayoumi said he had the diagram because he liked finding equations and could not remember when he had written it. By the evening of 22 September 2001, copies of the plane diagram were in London in the hands of both the FBI and UK counter-terror police - and just metres from the custody suite where Omar al-Bayoumi was being questioned. Records show they passed through at least three further FBI agents in the following two days. But here, the mystery begins. The FBI briefed the Met officers to question Bayoumi about the other high-priority exhibits, but the detectives in the custody suite were never given, or briefed about, the plane diagram. Many FBI agents have told us the immediate aftermath of 9/11 was a round-the-clock frenzy. But it is hard to understand how a piece of evidence of this importance, in a case being handled with considerable urgency, was not put into the hands of the interviewing detectives. The FBI declined to respond to our questions. The Metropolitan Police told us it could not comment because of the ongoing legal case. Carrier bags of video tapes Soon after the plane diagram was couriered to Paddington Green, all Bayoumi's videos, including the footage of the paintballing, were taken from Birmingham to New Scotland Yard for copying. By 24 September, the custody suite a mile or so away at Paddington Green had access to the video cassettes. The detectives brought the bags of tapes into the room where Bayoumi was being questioned - and some of the footage was played to him. He was asked about two tapes featuring a gathering, but the British officers were not briefed by the FBI to ask him about the video of the paintballing session - nor about his association with Anwar al-Awlaki. On the day he would need to be charged or released, the Met detectives joined a conference call with several senior officials from the US Department of Justice and FBI. Panorama and Radio 4 have spoken to two participants at the meeting. One recalls the British detectives setting out the evidence they believed met the threshold for the Americans to extradite Bayoumi to face charges in the US. The response from the DOJ officials was that no extradition would be sought because there was insufficient evidence. On 28 September 2001, Bayoumi was released. But, at that point, the FBI had not shipped all of the evidence found in Birmingham back to the US, let alone exhaustively analysed it. One memorandum from the FBI's legal attache in London, sent two weeks later, noted there were a "number of videos, floppy disks and documentation still to be viewed". 'We've convicted people for less' After Omar al-Bayoumi's release, agents continued analysing the evidence against him. The BBC understands the plane diagram was couriered from London for analysis at the New York Field Office, which was in overall charge of the 9/11 investigation. But we have not been able to trace any records of this analysis or its conclusions. A 2021 Presidential order required the FBI to declassify files relating to its 9/11 investigations, including into Bayoumi. However, of the files released, the FBI has only produced one document referring to the diagram, despite its evidential significance, and this was only created 11 years after the diagram's initial discovery in 2001. The diagram seems to have fallen into a black hole. It was not passed on to San Diego, where Bayoumi had lived in the USA and where the FBI Field Office was also investigating him. In fact, San Diego - where agents were interviewing his associates, searching his mosque, analysing his telephone records and bank statements - received almost none of the large volume of evidence seized by the Met Police in Birmingham. Rick Lambert, who ran the FBI's investigation there, told the BBC his office made repeated requests to New York to send copies of all the evidence. "Their position was, we're in charge of the case; we'll send it to you when we're finished analysing." Lambert said New York did not comply his office's requests. "I believe there is the potential that had we received that evidence and analysed it, that we would have been able to put the pieces of the puzzle together much more quickly." Documents show that, in spring 2002, the San Diego office was ultimately able to get copies of a handful of videos by obtaining them not from New York, but from the FBI liaison in London. What happened to the paintballing video is equally curious. A copy of the tape was sent to the FBI office in New York, where it was viewed, one agent told us. But it was not included in the office's summaries documenting Bayoumi's extremist connections. FBI and DOJ memos from 2002, viewed by the BBC, discussed materials seized from Bayoumi's homes in Birmingham that could "demonstrate Omar al-Bayoumi's anti-American sentiments and beliefs" and writings by Bayoumi himself that "can be interpreted as jihadist". But there was no mention of the paintballing video or Bayoumi's connection to Anwar al-Awlaki. Jeffrey Breinholt, then the deputy director of counter-terrorism at the Department of Justice who oversaw prosecutors working on terrorism charges after 9/11, told the BBC that Bayoumi's name had come up "as one of the hot possibilities for charges". But he said the New York Attorney's Office never sent charges to him or his colleagues for approval. If they had, the plane diagram would have been significant evidence against Bayoumi, he said. "We've convicted people for less." The paintballing video, Breinholt told us, is another "very telling bit of evidence" with the presence of Anwar al-Awlaki being "pretty damn significant". "As a manager who reviewed a lot of proposed terrorism cases over the years, I can tell you that that would have jumped out. I think it would be a material support charge against Bayoumi." There were no charges brought against Bayoumi. Agents who tried to investigate Omar al-Bayoumi encountered other roadblocks. In October 2001 in San Diego, Lambert and colleagues wanted to interview a number of Saudi officials in the US - many connected to the Ministry of Islamic Affairs - who they suspected had co-ordinated the help Bayoumi gave to two of the hijackers, Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar. Because diplomats have a special protected status, the agents needed permission from FBI headquarters and the State Department. "The answer came back, 'no, you're not going to do that'," Lambert, who is now a consultant for the 9/11 families in their lawsuit, told us. Agents in Los Angeles experienced a similar outcome the following year, when they applied to interview a Saudi religious diplomat Bayoumi had met immediately after his first encounter with Hazmi and Mihdhar in the city. "We hit a roadblock so hard, I think we all had airbag burns," said Steve Moore, who oversaw the FBI's 9/11 investigation in LA. Moore says his team made repeated requests to interview the official, but permission never came. Like the FBI, the State Department declined to comment. A multi-course dinner with Saudi secret police In October 2003, the 9/11 Commission - set up by Congress to provide a "full and complete" account of the attacks - interviewed Omar al-Bayoumi in Riyadh. He had returned to Saudi Arabia in the months after his release by British police. The interview was conducted, in the presence of Saudi secret police, by the Commission's executive director Philip Zelikow, a former advisor to President George W Bush, along with a senior staffer and an agent from FBI headquarters. The Commission's notes from the time record that Bayoumi was given a remarkable degree of reassurance during the interview. He "was told that no-one believes he knowingly helped the hijackers carry out their terrorist mission". Bayoumi indignantly said he was a peace-lover who had become "a victim of the victims". During the interview, the delegation broke away for a multi-course dinner hosted by the Mabahith, the secret police, without Bayoumi. After the interview concluded, the Mabahith told the American delegation they "would like to see him cleared". The Americans responded that no exoneration would be possible before their report was published. When the 9/11 Commission Report was published in July 2004, Bayoumi was, in effect, cleared. It described him as "obliging and gregarious" and stated there was no evidence he had extremist views. But some staff on the Commission were not convinced of Bayoumi's innocence, and thought it likely he knew Hazmi and Mihdhar were al Qaeda operatives. The BBC can reveal that those staff objected to a line in the report concluding that he was "an unlikely candidate for clandestine involvement with Islamist extremists". In the end, a compromise was agreed, and this conclusion was attributed to "our investigators who have dealt directly with him and studied his background". The line was written based on the four and a half hours the Commission delegation had spent with Bayoumi, which included the interruption for dinner. The Commission never saw the plane diagram, the paintballing video, written evidence of Bayoumi's alleged extremism, or much of the rest of the evidence the Met Police had seized. Philip Zelikow did not answer the specific questions we asked him. He told the BBC the 9/11 Commission's findings had been subject to two government reviews, in 2015 and 2021, and the Commission had been "open about our suspicions and uncertainties. We were careful about whom to accuse of complicity in mass murder." The Department of Justice told us it was unable to comment on matters and decisions from 25 years ago, involving staff who no longer worked there. The head of the FBI's 9/11 investigation, Mary Galligan, has previously stated the Commission had "access to everything". We tried to contact Omar al-Bayoumi through the Saudi government, but he did not respond. He has previously denied knowing Hazmi and Mihdhar were hijackers, that he was a Saudi spy, and that he had any involvement in 9/11. The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia did not respond to our request for comment. It has previously said any allegation that Saudi Arabia or its officials are complicit in 9/11 is categorically false.

item.title: Kyiv air raid alerts at record high as Russia launches round-the-clock strikes
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjdvx9pz44ro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Kyiv air raid alerts at record high as Russia launches round-the-clock strikes - Published Kyiv is suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, according to BBC Verify analysis of government figures. Most air attacks used to come at night but Russia's new tactic of striking Ukraine's capital during the day is causing huge disruption to schools and businesses. The round the clock attacks have forced people to head for shelter as many as 13 times a day, with air raid alerts lasting from a few minutes to nearly four and a half hours. Residents in Kyiv are struggling to adapt to this new reality, adding to existing stress and anxiety. The alerts force pupils to leave their classrooms and workers their offices and leave commuters struggling to get home as overland trains stop. This has forced the government to plan a new, two-tier warning system that allows people to carry on working, travelling and studying depending on the scale of the threat. There was a brief pause in attacks on Kyiv over the weekend while US envoys were in town for talks about trying to end the war. But analysis of figures from the state-owned app Kyiv digital shows that since the round-the-clock Russian attacks began at the end of August, air raid sirens have sounded across Kyiv's skies on average 10 times a day. In the seven days from Thursday 27 August, Kyiv endured 76 air raid alerts. The largest comparable number in 2022 was the week beginning 27 February when there were around 66 alerts. Absolute comparisons are not possible because data gathered in the first few days of the invasion was sometimes incomplete. But the trend shown by the numbers is clear. From the BBC's office, we hear the near constant rumble of air defences and drone explosions. The more frequent Russian strikes are exacerbated by a second development, the use of newer and faster attack drones powered by jet engines. Some of these fly almost 370 mph (595 km/h), three times as fast the older Shahed drones driven by propellers, and are harder to shoot down. Ukraine's air force says Russia launched 2,800 fast drones in August, almost twice as many as in July. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has held an emergency meeting with ministers and commanders to work out how to produce new high-speed missiles that can intercept the faster Russian drones. "You can all see that the Russians have changed the tactics of their strikes against Ukraine and, since August, have been terrorising our people, our cities and our villages far more intensely," the president said. Diplomats say the risk is that Russia will manufacture its fast attack drones more quickly than Ukraine can develop a new generation of interceptors. Some military sources say this threat could become far greater than Russia's ballistic missiles which have largely overcome Ukraine's depleted Patriot defences. Ukraine uses warplanes, anti-aircraft guns and shoulder-launched missiles to try to bring down the jet-powered drones. But Yurii Ihnat, spokesman for the Ukrainian Air Force, said only about 60 percent of the drones were being shot down and they needed new interceptors to tackle the threat. "The task now is to make them faster and equip them with specialised guidance systems so that they can shoot down jet-powered UAVs, the jet-powered Shaheds," he said. "The key issue really is having guidance systems, because that is one of the crucial elements. It is not enough for the interceptor simply to fly fast — it has to hit the target. That is very important." Analysts say Russia's aim is not only to weaken Kyiv's morale but also damage Ukraine's economy by targeting businesses and warehouses. The alerts are also disrupting the start of the new academic year and forcing school children to leave their classrooms throughout the day. When another air raid began, some students at the Drahomanov Ukrainian State University in central Kyiv headed underground; others stayed chatting on the street, such is the normality of these alerts. Diana, a student teacher, said she did not sleep well at night and her schedule was disrupted during the day. "Sometimes it is hard because most of the day I need to go to safe places, like the metro or somewhere underground," she said. "It's a terrible time, but thank God we are alive. We go day by day." Ihor, studying to become a chemistry teacher, said he was used to the alerts after many years of war but life was still hard. "We are annoyed by the sirens because they are constant," he said. "It destroys the quality of our education… We cannot study normally." After a drone attack in a residential part of central Kyiv, students from a nearby school were evacuated for fear of explosions or a secondary, so-called "double-tap" attack. Sophia, 17, told us it was very sad but this is what life was like now. "It's a little bit scary to live here in Kyiv," she said. "It's very difficult." The interview was then interrupted by another siren. "We need to go," she said. "It is very dangerous for you to stand in the streets. Maybe we can have a second detonation." The constant air raids are a huge problem for businesses, many of which have to shut their doors every time a siren wails. We saw crowds of shop workers from Kyiv's biggest department store hanging around the streets during an alert, forced to leave their work place but not fearful enough to seek shelter. There is also disruption to public transport. Some metro trains have to stop during an alert because they travel overground across the Dnipro river that bisects the city. This causes chaos for commuters who are forced to get on replacement buses. To minimise this disruption, the government has agreed a new air-raid warning system with two different threat levels. A yellow warning to indicate a drone attack with less threat and fewer restrictions on work and travel. A red warning to indicate a more dangerous missile attack with more severe constraints on activity. As ever, Ukraine is adapting to a yet another new threat. But the fear is that Russia's constant attacks now may leave the country and its capital less prepared for what many expect to be a tough winter as Russia shifts its attack back to Ukraine's energy infrastructure. item.title: Austria's Islamic headscarf ban in force as under-14s go back to school
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyz74xn8q8o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Austria's Islamic headscarf ban in force as under-14s go back to school - Published As the new school year begins in Austria, a law banning headscarves in schools for girls under 14 has gone into force. The law forbids "traditional Muslim" head coverings, such as hijabs or burkas, in public and private schools across the country. Integration Minister Claudia Bauer, from the conservative People's Party (ÖVP), says the headscarf is "a sign of oppression and a means of controlling girls from the earliest childhood". But critics say the new law is fuelling anti-Muslim feeling in the country and could be unconstitutional. The law was brought in by the conservative-led coalition of three centrist parties, the ÖVP, the Social Democrats (SPÖ) and the liberal Neos. They say the law is a "clear commitment to gender equality" and is intended to protect the rights of young girls. Carla Amina Baghajati, from the official Islamic Community in Austria (IGGÖ), told the BBC that the organisation "firmly opposes the ban". "We believe it unjustifiably restricts the fundamental right to freedom of religion and disproportionately affects Muslim girls," she said. "Rather than protecting children, it singles out a specific religious practice and risks excluding the very children it claims to support." The IGGÖ said it would support legal challenges by girls and their families "who believe that their fundamental rights are being infringed" and who wished to bring their cases before the Constitutional Court. The court struck down a previous ban on headscarves in primary schools in 2020 on the basis that it contravened the principle of Austria's religious neutrality. Teachers are expected to enforce the new ban if they see a child wearing a headscarf by holding a series of talks with the student and their legal guardians. If there are repeated violations, child services must be notified and as a last resort, guardians could face fines of up to €800 (£685). Some teachers have expressed concerns about having to enforce the ban. The Green Party's Sigi Maurer accused Education Minister Christoph Wiederkehr, from the liberal NEOS, of "creating new conflicts and offloading them onto the teachers". She said teachers were "already under enormous strain" and that Wiederkehr wanted to "foist the role of police officers onto them" on top of their other duties. The opposition far-right Freedom Party (FPÖ) says the current ban doesn't go far enough. It is calling for a general prohibition on headscarves and face coverings in schools for students and teachers alike. The FPÖ's Ricarda Berger said there was "no place for political Islam in Austria, and certainly not in our schools". Austria's Chancellor Christian Stocker, leader of the ÖVP, recently called for a constitutional ban on political Islam, telling Austrian public broadcaster ORF he did not "want to live in an Islamic state". In France there has been a ban on wearing any conspicuous religious symbols, including headscarves, turbans and kippas, in schools for more than 20 years. The Austrian law differs from French legislation in that it specifically targets head coverings worn by Muslim women. Austria, like several other European countries including France, Belgium and Denmark, bans the full face veil (niqabs or burkas) in public. Baghajati said the IGGÖ was concerned about "a troubling trend" across Europe "in which complex social challenges are reduced to symbolic measures aimed at minority groups." "Such approaches may generate political attention, but they rarely solve the underlying problems," she said.

item.title: Burundians rush to leave Kenya ahead of crackdown on unregistered traders
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c158wwl22xko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Burundians rush to leave Kenya ahead of crackdown on unregistered traders - Published Hundreds of Burundians in Kenya are scrambling to process travel documents to leave the country ahead of the crackdown on unlicensed small businesses run by migrants. Kenyan President William Ruto set Monday as the deadline for foreigners operating small-scale businesses to cease work, after the trade ministry said some exploited visa rules to work without the required permits. Long queues were seen outside Burundi's embassy in the capital Nairobi after it said it would offer free emergency travel documents to citizens who want to go back home. Others are racing to buy bus tickets. Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of migrants from across East Africa seeking work and business opportunities. Kenya's trade ministry said there had been "deliberate misuse of visa applications by some visitors", who arrived as investors or tourists but got involved in business activities that breached their declared status. According to the United Nations refugee agency, there are around 16,000 Burundian refugees and asylum seekers in Kenya. It is unclear how many are involved in small-scale trading or how many would be affected by the crackdown. Burundians have been seen carrying all their belongings - from suitcases to mattresses - as they try to leave ahead of the crackdown, but some of them said they could not afford the cost of travel and urged the Kenyan government to extend the deadline. Ruto's directive follows a similar crackdown in Tanzania last year and rising anti‑migrant sentiment in South Africa. Burundi's Foreign Affairs Minister Edouard Bizimana said in a post on X that "Kenyans in Burundi were living peacefully but if the hate speech against Burundi continues things will certainty change". "Kenya government is responsible for the lives of Burundians living in Kenya," he added. His comments came after Ruto last week said that while Kenya remained open to foreign investment, it could not be "that a person comes from China or elsewhere to be a hawker or open a small shop". He argued that investors should create jobs and expand production rather than compete with Kenyans in small businesses. Ruto's comments sparked mixed reactions, with some critics describing them as a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia. Government officials deny the allegation. Some foreign nationals say they fear for their safety, while police have warned Kenyans against targeting them. Bizimana's post followed an urgent meeting he held with representatives of the East African Community (EAC), an eight-member bloc which promotes economic integration in the region. Both Kenya and Burundi are part of the group. Kenyan representatives attended the meeting called by Bizimana in Burundi. Bizimana said he had asked the Kenyan ambassador to convey to his government Burundi's concerns and to ensure that no Burundian was subjected to abuse. On Sunday, a top official in Kenya's foreign affairs ministry said foreigners, with the required documentation, including "work permits and licences", could continue their activities. "Burundian nationals and all East Africans - and Africans for that matter - are free to live in Kenya as long as they conduct their businesses or work according to the requirements of our laws, Permanent Secretary Korir Sing'oei said. The government's clarification, however, did little to ease concerns among some foreign traders. Alexis Ntinanirwa, the head of the Association of Burundians living in Kenya, told the BBC Great Lakes service that he was unhappy with Ruto's decision, but was urging Burundians to remain patient. He warned that the issue could have wider regional consequences because Kenyans are also involved in small-scale businesses in other East African countries. "This issue is not only going to cause problems for Burundians working in Kenya, but it is also going to cause problems in the region because there are also Kenyans doing these small jobs in our countries in Burundi, Tanzania and Uganda." Ntinanirwa advised Burundians involved in hawking and other small businesses to avoid confrontation with police. item.title: Indonesia volcano eruption leaves 340,000 stranded as airports extend closure
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czezydp4l97o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Indonesia volcano eruption leaves 340,000 stranded as airports extend closure - Published More than 340,000 passengers have been left stranded across Indonesia after a volcanic eruption disrupted nearly 3,000 flights and forced airports to suspend operations for a second day. Anak Krakatau, located 150km (90mi) from Jakarta, began erupting late on Friday, producing lava fountains and sending volcanic ash into the capital and the Lampung province. It stayed seismically active throughout the weekend. Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International airport decided not to reopen at 18:00 (11:00 GMT) as planned due to the continued presence of volcanic ash near its airspace. Flights will instead resume at 23:59 on Monday, the airport has said in a statement. Halim Perdanakusuma, a smaller airport that caters to civil and military flights, will also remain closed until then. Snaking queues formed at the departure halls in Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on Monday as stranded passengers sought refunds and tried to get updates on when they would be able to fly. Finna, who was supposed to fly home to Jakarta from Malang, a city in East Java, on Sunday morning, described the frezny at the airport as flights got repeatedly rescheduled. "It was very crowded because passengers from the morning flights had piled up, while those scheduled for later departures still didn't know what would happen," the 46-year-old told BBC Indonesian. "We were all glued to the flight information screens." Not wanting to deal with the uncertainty, Finna eventually spent the night on two intercity trains before arriving in Jakarta at 03:00 on Monday. "Everyone seems to be racking their brains [figuring alternative transportation options]", said Jo Shaw, who was visiting Indonesia with members of her conservation charity Save the Rhino International. Shaw's team had axed their plans to camp out at Java's Ujung Kulon National Park after authorities raised its alert level for the Anak Krakatau volcano. "Being stranded in an airport hotel is a relatively minor inconvenience to be resolved in a few days hopefully," Shaw said, adding that she was more concerned about the teams working on the ground with the rhinos under such environmental conditions. A newly wed Malaysian couple who had just spent a week in Bali said they were told that the next flight back to Kuala Lumpur wouldn't be until 11 September. "What are we going to do here for another five days? We only prepared enough money for our honeymoon and [were supposed] to go home yesterday," Amir Hamzah told Malaysia's national news agency Bernama. "We thought we would just sleep at the airport for a few hours and then take the morning flight home [on Monday]. We never thought we would end up being stuck here for days," the 29-year-old said. On Monday, Indonesia's Geological Agency warned that "the probability of further eruptions in the coming periods remains high". Volcanic ash reached as high as 6,000m on the Java side of the volcano and 15,000m on the Sumatra side and in some parts of Java's westernmost province Banten, the meteorological agency BMKG said. Anak Krakatau sits on the Sunda Strait about midway between the islands of Java and Sumatra. The most recent eruption occurred at 20:23 on Sunday, according to the agency. "We cannot ascertain when this will end due to the dynamic weather," Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said in relation to the temporary closures of the affected airports. Dudy said on Sunday that authorities across the airports have been conducting tests every 30 minutes "to anticipate whether the ash spread is widening or subsiding". Authorities have warned against approaching or engaging in activities within a 3km radius from the active crater, while ships passing through the Sunda Strait have also been prohibited from entering an exclusion zone of 3km radius from it. Authorities have also confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano. Anak Krakatau, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa. The volcano collapsed in December 2018 triggering a huge tsunami which killed over 400 people, and displaced and injured thousands more on the nearby coastlines of Sumatra and Java. Scientists found that some of the chunks of rock that slid from the volcano when it collapsed were about 70-90m high. The Pacific Ring of Fire refers to a string of volcanoes, earthquake sites and tectonic plates around the Pacific. It spreads across 40,000km (25,000 miles) from the southern tip of South America all the way to New Zealand. Roughly 90% of all earthquakes occur along the area and the ring is dotted with 75% of all active volcanoes on Earth, that's 452 individual active volcanoes. With reporting by Farida Susanty in Jakarta and Koh Ewe in Singapore - Published1 day ago

item.title: Tanzanian President Samia's husband dies in hospital
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgqd774wzpdo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Tanzanian President Samia's husband dies in hospital - Published The husband of Tanzania's President Samia Suluhu Hassan, Hafidh Ameir Hassan, has died while receiving treatment at a hospital in Zanzibar. Vice-president Deogratius Ndejembi - who made the official announcement of Ameir's death - said he had been suffering from a heart condition. He was buried at his family's residence in Kizimkazi, a village on the country's semi-autonomous island of Zanzibar, on Monday evening. Ameir was an agricultural academic who largely kept a low public profile. He became Tanzania's first First Gentleman after President Samia took office in 2021. In his announcement, Ndejembi said Ameir died at 08:00 local time (06:00 GMT) on Monday at the Emilio Mzena Memorial Hospital. The vice-president led tributes as he conveyed his condolences to Samia, as well as Ameir's family and friends. Kenyan President William Ruto said he received the news of his passing with "deep sorrow". "President Samia has lost a lifelong companion, her children a beloved father, and Tanzania a distinguished son," he wrote on social media. Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema also shared his condolences, saying that they "stand side by side" with the first family, and all of Tanzania during "this difficult time". Similarly, Burundi's President Évariste Ndayishimiye paid his respects and prayed for Samia and her family to have "comfort and strength in this difficult moment". "May he [God] grant eternal rest to the soul of Hafidh Ameir Hassan," he added. The First Gentleman rarely appeared in public alongside the president. He was only occasionally seen with her at official events. He married Samia in 1978, before she entered national politics. The couple had four children - three sons and a daughter - together. item.title: China to pump $54bn into state banks and insurers to boost economy
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2z37qj4wno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
China to pump $54bn into state banks and insurers to boost economy - Published China is pumping tens of billions of dollars into eight state-owned banks and insurance companies to help shore up the country's financial system and boost its slowing economy. The cash injection, which is being led by China's finance ministry, will total 360 billion yuan ($53.6bn; £39.7bn), state news agency Xinhua said on Sunday. The outlet said the move "will help further enhance their sound operating capabilities, risk resistance capabilities, and ability to serve the real economy". It marks the latest move in Beijing's attempts to reinvigorate the world's second largest economy as it faces issues including trade tensions with the West, the impact of the Iran war and an aging population. The package will boost the finances of three big lenders and five insurers including the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, the Agricultural Bank of China and China Export & Credit Insurance Corporation. State news outlet Global Times said this "will give banks and financial institutions more resources to channel into credit for the real economy, while strengthening their ability to withstand external shocks at a time of global financial uncertainty". President Xi Jinping has long seen financial stability as key to China's national security. This weekend's announcements come as Beijing is aiming to reshape the economy in the face of a number of challenges such as a shrinking workforce, a years-long property market slump and ongoing trade and technology rivalry with the US. China's economic growth slowed sharply between the start of April and end of June as weak domestic demand and the Iran war's impact on oil prices overshadowed the country's strong exports. Official gross domestic product (GDP) figures released in July showed China's economy grew in the second quarter by 4.3%, below Beijing's annual target, and after a 5% rise in the first quarter. In March, Beijing cut the growth target to a range of 4.5%-5%, its lowest economic expansion goal since 1991, a move some analysts say has given Beijing space to acknowledge pre-existing economic weakness.
