item.title: Rescuers dig through debris as seven dead in building collapse in Delhi
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8r6ezx1jmro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Rescuers dig through debris as seven dead in building collapse in Delhi - Published Rescuers are digging through the rubble a day after a residential building collapsed in the Indian capital, Delhi, killing at least seven people. It's not clear how many people were inside the five-storey building in south-west Delhi - or if there are still people under the debris. Eyewitnesses told local media on Sunday that two-to-four dozen people were inside, but no official numbers have been shared. Authorities have confirmed 12 people were taken to hospital and that seven died while others are receiving treatment. Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta said "accumulation of water, combined with ongoing repair work in the basement" of the building, Hostel Daze, caused the collapse. The building owner has been arrested and five senior civic officials of Delhi Municipal Corporation (MCD) have been suspended following the tragedy, Gupta added. The building in the Satya Niketan neighbourhood of south-west Delhi, which sits a short distance from Delhi University's south campus which has five colleges, came down around 13:30 local time (08:00 GMT) on Sunday. A majority of the residents were students and many were thought to be in their rooms at the time of the collapse as there were no lessons on Sunday. On Monday morning, Gupta said "approximately 80% of the debris had been cleared" from the building, and "only the rubble from the basement remains". The BBC found the area around the site of the collapse cordoned off and teeming with rescue workers in bright orange uniforms. An excavator dug through the rubble in the hope of finding survivors amidst a pile of bricks. In another corner, a few mattresses half covered in debris were lying in a pile. The smell of burning metal was overpowering as teams of the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) could be seen using electric saws to cut through iron grills, penetrating layers and layers of steel and concrete. There is no confirmation if there are still people under the debris or if there are more survivors. Hospital officials are not saying whether the casualties include students, local residents or labourers who were working in the basement. On Sunday, a local legislative assembly member at the scene said that some of the trapped students had been making calls from under the rubble. An eyewitness who was at his shop nearby when the tragedy struck told news agency ANI that the building collapse sounded "like the rumble of an earthquake". "We rushed out immediately; there was a lot of smoke and dust here. The entire building had collapsed. Some bodies were recovered, and they also rescued four students who were still breathing." He said he could hear students crying out from under the rubble saying "save us, save us!" Gupta said an adjacent building had been evacuated "as a precautionary measure" - and local media reports say it would be demolished on Monday. "Every possible effort is being made to safely rescue those trapped," she added. Delhi Police said the building had only been 40 or 50 years old. The owner of a nearby shop told ANI that it had been under a 100-year lease and that the leaseholder had undertaken excavation work in the basement to expand the hostel and increase their income. A civic official said they were trying to ascertain whether any digging or structural work was carried out in the building recently, Times of India reported., external "Given the incessant rain, we are examining the possibility of seepage weakening the structure. Repair or other work could also have contributed to the collapse. At this stage, however, it is difficult to establish the exact cause," he said. Police have registered a case against the owner of the building and are searching for him. The National Students' Union of India called on the government to investigate the cause of the collapse and hold anyone found responsible to account. "Negligence with the safety of students and common people will not be tolerated at any cost," it said. Satya Niketan is a densely populated area which houses a large student population, with a number of hostels in the neighbourhood. Many students who come from outside Delhi to attend South Campus colleges are forced to live in cheap private hostels and paying-guest (PG) accommodations due to a lack of hostel facilities on campus. "There are 75 students in Sociology Honours class, but only two get a seat in the college hostel. All other students have to live here," Sawai Sharma, a student of Venkateswara College, told BBC News Hindi. Sharma, who often visited a friend who lived in the building and narrowly escaped the accident, said a bed in the building cost 18,000 rupees ($190; £140) a month, making it affordable for students. Another student, Shivam Yadav, said a friend of his lived in the building and was in his room at the time of the accident. "He was on the third floor at the time of the accident. He has been rescued and sent to hospital." Yadav said that most of the buildings in Satya Niketan are "overloaded". "The buildings are in a dilapidated condition. No inspections are conducted. There are no rules or guidelines here." College student Ankit Tiwari said conditions at these hostels and PGs "are appalling". "Students are paying a lot for a very small space which they share with others. There is no proper water or sewage facility here." Tiwari, who lives nearby, reached the site about half an hour after the collapse. "Students were helping each other as we came first, before the rescue teams arrived. What we saw was tragic. We have been finding books, mangled desks and study notes," he said. Building collapses are relatively common in Delhi, with more than a thousand recorded in the past three years causing dozens of deaths, according to fire department figures. Poor foundations, inadequate materials and unqualified construction workers were among the common reasons for collapses. Eleven people, including three children, were reportedly killed last April when a residential building collapsed in north-eastern Delhi. In 2024, three students drowned after getting trapped in the flooded basement of an exam coaching centre in capital Delhi, sparking anger and protests. Additional reporting from Aleks Phillips - Published28 June 2024

item.title: How significant are AfD's historic gains for Germany and the rest of Europe?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c986w38r4j5o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
How significant are AfD's historic gains for Germany and the rest of Europe? - Published "Seismic", "a socio-political earthquake", "a watershed moment for Germany". This was how political analysts and many media outlets described the stunning victory of the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in local elections in Germany on Sunday. Is that an exaggeration? Saxony-Anhalt is one of the smallest of massive Germany's 16 regions. It boasts a mere 1.7 million out of 59 million eligible voters nationwide. How significant can its political sentiments be, especially since the AfD narrowly failed to win an outright majority? The answer: Very significant. First and foremost, at home in Germany. The vote may have been regional but it impacts at national level. The AfD landslide piles even more pressure on the already beleaguered centrist coalition government in Berlin. It may prove to be the nail in the political coffin of Germany's deeply unpopular conservative Chancellor, Friedrich Merz. He had promised to slash the AfD's popularity. These political woes will further weaken and distract Germany, the EU's most powerful player, at a time of continental crisis - as Europe struggles to contain Russian aggression, US President Donald Trump's tariff tantrums and the economic threat from China. The Saxony-Anhalt result also provokes soul-searching throughout Germany, where the Nazi past still looms large. This is the first outstanding electoral landslide for a hard-right nationalist party - giving it a real shot at governing, in this case, at regional level - since the fall of the Third Reich in 1945. The German authorities have labelled the AfD, in part, anti-democratic and a number of regional factions of the party, including Saxony-Anhalt, far-right extremist. The AfD is well-known to be particularly popular in east Germany but it is now also polling as the biggest political party nationwide. Germany's political mainstream has failed voters, it would seem. What does Europe's biggest single economy, its most populous nation not counting Russia, do now? Trump interest in the AfD Tiny Saxony-Anhalt is causing waves outside Germany, too. None other than the US president swiftly posted the Saxony-Anhalt exit poll on his Truth Social platform on Sunday. The AfD's anti-immigration, anti-woke, "Germany for Germans" message chimes closely with Donald Trump's Maga [Make America Great Again] missive. Along with a number of other nationalist parties in Europe, the AfD borrows heavily from the Trump playbook - undermining mainstream media, questioning the neutrality of judges and promising to "make Germany great again". Interesting to note though - the US president is rarely name-checked on the campaign trail in Europe. Politicians are keenly aware just how unpopular he is amongst voters. Hot on Donald Trump's social media heels on Sunday night was the influential Russian businessman Kirill Dmitriev, CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund. He declared the AfD result "historic", Germany's national government "discredited" and the German chancellor "humiliated", comparing Friedrich Merz to the UK's not-long-gone Prime Minister, Keir Starmer, who felt forced to resign this summer. Why Russia has skin in the game What interest might Russia have in German regional elections, you might ask, and what was Dmitriev's dig at the UK all about? The German government is the largest single donor to Ukraine and the UK is known to have provided Kyiv with missiles used to strike inside Russian territory. This has deeply angered Moscow. The AfD, by comparison, is pretty pro-Russia. It wants to stop sending military aid to Ukraine, halt sanctions against Moscow and start buying much cheaper Russian energy again. Energy-hungry German industry suffered a huge economic blow after the country halted Russian energy imports, following Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The AfD's softly-softly approach to Russia has another appeal in Germany's east, which remains far poorer than the west. This, despite Germany spending between 2.3 and 3tn (£2tn-£2.6tn) - depending on reports and whether inflation is taken into account - to help integrate the former Communist part of the country after the 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall. Saxony-Anhalt is Germany's poorest region and there, as in much of east Germany, you often encounter what's known as "Ostalgie" amongst voters; essentially "nostalgia in the east" for comparatively more stable times under Communism. Parties across Europe respond Also watching the Saxony-Anhalt election closely was the European Union. The next 12 months is bumper election season across the EU. Ballots are expected in key nations France, Italy, Spain and Poland. Brussels fears more "extreme" parties, left but particularly right of the political spectrum, may benefit across the board. The leader of Spain's nationalist Vox party, Santiago Abascal, posted on X on Sunday that the AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt was " a great hope for Germany and for Europe". By contrast, France's Europe Minister, Benjamin Haddad, an ally of centrist President Emmanuel Macron, warned "this is a serious moment in Europe, seeing the far-right win in a regional election in Germany". Neither the AfD, nor other European parties labelled "extreme right" or "hard right", accept the label. They also differ from one another in tone and party programme. France's National Rally under Marine Le Pen kicked the AfD out of its grouping in the European Parliament two years ago, for being too "radical". What the parties do tend to share, however, is an anti-immigration platform and strong nationalist messaging. And that really worries the EU. Whether it is a rallying cry for "Germany First" or "Italy First" or "France for the French!", the concern in Brussels is that the rise of nationalist parties strains European cohesion at a time when outside events demand it more than ever. Nationalist parties like the AfD or Italy's League Party tend to be deeply Eurosceptic, but Brussels says Europe needs to stand united to counter Donald Trump's bullying, for example, or to effectively protect European business against China's goods dumping. Europe's defence establishment also warns that fractures in European sanctions against Russia or countries going tepid on Nato membership (as you see in Marine Le Pen's National Rally for example, or Germany's AfD) just emboldens Moscow. Security chiefs say nations must stick together to stop Russia in Ukraine, otherwise the Kremlin will be tempted to attack inside Nato, such as the Baltic states. The thing is, Europe's voters are very aware of these outside threats and the impact they have at home. They worry about the impact of wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, about crumbling health services at home and dwindling economic security for themselves and their families. Uncontrolled immigration and safety on the streets are huge concerns, too. And this is where the significance of the Saxony-Anhalt vote shines bright - a flashing red warning to traditional political parties, but also to institutions across Europe like the judiciary and security services. Those the AfD dismisses as the self-interested "Establishment". Voters on this continent feel lost and let down by parties they have supported over and again for decades. Looking right or left now at election time does not mean they have all suddenly become extremist. The AfD campaign slogan in Saxony-Anhalt was an upbeat "Anything is Possible!" - plus a promise to make Germans feel proud of their country again. Till now untried and untested in government, people seem increasingly willing to give them a go. - Germany's far-right AfD set for big win in eastern state, just short of majority - Published12 hours ago - AfD celebrate projected win in Saxony-Anhalt - Published1 day ago Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. item.title: Peace talks rich in symbolism but fundamental differences between Russia and Ukraine remain
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c980j5m8mpro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Peace talks rich in symbolism but fundamental differences between Russia and Ukraine remain - Published The talks in Kyiv were rich in symbolism. The sight of Donald Trump's envoys setting foot on Ukrainian soil for the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion. The fact they had to travel by train because they could not risk flying and running the gauntlet of Russian drones - weapons launched on the orders of the man at whose table they sat in the Kremlin only hours ago. The symbolism of Ukrainian President Zelensky greeting Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at Kyiv's Saint Sophia Cathedral, not only an icon of Ukraine's ancient history, but also just a few yards from where Russian drones hit the headquarters of the country's security services on Friday. You did not have to join too many dots to work out the point Zelensky was making. Both sides held talks for several hours; they were later joined by some European national security advisers, including the UK's National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell. And afterwards, all sides spoke warmly of having held substantive discussions. They spoke hopefully of reviving past "trilateral talks" involving both the US and Europe. But fundamental differences remain. The US envoys had come hot foot from Moscow where Vladimir Putin had told them Russia was making "tangible advances" on the battlefield. The story they heard from Ukraine was different, in fact the opposite. Ukrainian officials claim that in August they gained more territory than they lost and Russia suffered 42,000 casualties, dead or wounded. Putin had also told the US envoys the root causes of the conflict had to be addressed, shorthand for his longstanding strategic demands that Ukraine cede territory, abandon hopes of joining Nato and reduce the size of its army. After the talks, Zelensky insisted Ukraine would require "strong and clear" security guarantees, including a strong army. Nor did he give any sign of being willing to give up any territory in the eastern Donbas region, an issue he described dryly as "difficult". Witkoff insisted progress had been made and the ingredients for a settlement were there. But he admitted both sides would have to make compromises to narrow the differences between them. And right now, it is hard to see either side doing that. So for now, the expectation in Kyiv is that the fighting will continue and they will face a hard winter ahead. Some diplomats talk of a window of opportunity for a possible settlement next spring. Others are less optimistic. Zelensky thanked the US envoys for their visit because the short-term pause in air strikes agreed by both sides had given the people of Kyiv a brief respite. Few expect it to last for long. - Published30 December 2025 - Published3 days ago

item.title: How £725 game-show winnings kick-started Champions League coach's career
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/cvgy8w548yyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
How £725 game-show winnings kick-started Champions League coach's career - Published On Thursday, Valdas Dambrauskas will walk out at Old Trafford as manager of Sabah in the Champions League. The Lithuanian's career will come full circle, some 20 years since he made his first steps into coaching with Manchester United Soccer Schools. "This is beyond my imagination," Dambrauskas told BBC Sport. "To go through that tunnel on to that pitch. "I've been many times to Old Trafford with the kids, and now I'm going to come as a coach." This only scratches the surface of Dambrauskas' remarkable story. It begins with an appearance on the Lithuanian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?, Dambrauskas using his modest winnings to move to London and forge a career in football. It is a tale of casual jobs, a determination to succeed and a nomadic coaching career across Europe - which now brings the 49-year-old back to England in the Champions League with the Azerbaijani club. How a game show gave Dambrauskas his break As Sabah's players and staff celebrated reaching the Champions League two weeks ago, unbeknownst to Dambrauskas he was becoming a social media star. It all related to that appearance on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? in 2002. Not because he was on the show, but how he spent the money he won. "This is so long ago," said Dambrauskas with a wry smile. "A back-in-the-year story that really was forgotten. "And now suddenly everybody is speaking about this." Dambrauskas walked away with 4,000 litas (about £725). That might not sound like much, but it was six months' wages to the average Lithuanian. For Dambrauskas, the real story should be his career and not a game show. "Everybody now takes only this part, you know, about the money," Dambrauskas said. "But yes, it is a true story. "My idea was somehow I will try to go on these [coaching] courses to gain the coaching badge, maybe go back one day to Lithuania and start to work as a football coach." What began with Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? would map out his whole career. 'I was doing two, three, sometimes four jobs' Dambrauskas says he had known since the age of 12 he would not make it as a player, but coaching would keep him close to football. He arrived in London in August 2002 aged 25 on a student visa with limited English. What followed would be eight years of hard work where he would coach for community projects, at a semi-professional club, within professional youth programmes - and hold down multiple jobs while raising two children. In 2004 he enrolled on a course in sports science and coaching at London Metropolitan University, the first real step in his career. Then he started out coaching by volunteering with the Access to Sports Project for deprived children in Finsbury Park. He went on to work with London Tigers, a charitable community organisation which runs teams from junior level right through to semi-professional. Starting out as a volunteer, across five years he progressed to manage the first team in non-league football in the Spartan South Midlands League, FA Cup and FA Vase. Dambrauskas became the first Lithuanian to achieve a Uefa coaching licence through the London Football Association. "I went on every possible course, every possible conference, London Football Coaches Association meetings," Dambrauskas said. "Everywhere I could go just to gain some information, some knowledge, some extra diploma, extra course. "That was very important for me and I took my chances." He got his first break at a professional club when Manchester United Soccer Schools took a chance on him in 2004. Dambrauskas spent five years coaching on residential courses in the UK and in Europe. "That was the best thing that could happen in my life," Dambrauskas said. "I went through three or four interviews. I will be forever grateful to [Foundation chief executive] John Shiels, the way he gave me this chance, because I didn't have experience. "I'd never been in a place with so many great personalities as I got in the Manchester United Soccer Schools." After a short spell with Fulham, Dambrauskas moved to Brentford. He credits academy director Ose Aibangee as one of the biggest influences on his career, pushing his limits. All the while he was juggling home life and working multiple jobs to make ends meet. "I was a gardener, a handyman, doing newspaper rounds at the beginning, also polishing floors in a pub," Dambrauskas said. "So many jobs. Working in retail, and then as a sports development officer, then a sports development manager, and the central YMCA. "I was doing two, three, sometimes four jobs." As well as the trip to Manchester United this week, Sabah will complete their Champions League group games at Arsenal in January. This also feels like fate for Dambrauskas - one of the buildings at London Metropolitan University on Holloway Road overlooked Emirates Stadium. When asked about his time in England, Dambrauskas' face lights up. "When I hear this word 'England', it for me sounds like opportunities," Dambrauskas said. "It was really amazing. England gave me all this and I'll forever be grateful." From England to 13 trophies in five countries Dambrauskas was working three jobs - at Brentford, London Tigers and as a sports development manager - when the opportunity arose to coach full-time. It meant leaving England to return to Lithuania, champions Ekranas appointing him assistant first-team and reserve-team coach at the end of 2010. After four years at Ekranas he was named manager of Zalgiris Vilnius, Lithuania's biggest club, where his career really took off. Dambrauskas won two league titles, three Lithuanian Cups and two Lithuanian Super Cups across three seasons - including a treble in 2016. Then came a series of moves in which Dambrauskas took charge of eight teams over nine years in seven countries. First RFS, with whom he won the Latvian Cup, and then Gorica in Croatia. A third league title came with Bulgarian side Ludogorets Razgrad, along with another Super Cup and Europa League qualification. Dambrauskas then returned to Croatia with Hajduk Split, a time which he described as "absolutely amazing" as the club won the Croatian Cup - their first trophy for 10 years. Next up was a spell in Greece with OFI Crete, then Omonia in Cyprus - who qualified for the Conference League - and Diosgyori in Hungary. Finally, in the summer of 2025, he arrived at Sabah, the 10th club of his career. Dambrauskas completed the league and cup double in his first season, as the club won the title for the first time. It took his trophy tally to 13 across five countries. Next stop, the Champions League. Champions League 'beyond imagination' Dambrauskas had to navigate four knockout ties to get Sabah to the Champions League, and they are the only club to make it all the way through from the first qualifying round. Welsh club TNS, Finland's KuPS, Danish side Aarhus and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva were all knocked out. The final qualifying game was as dramatic as Dambrauskas' own story. Sabah were going out, then a goal by Tellur Mutallimov in the fourth minute of stoppage time sent the tie into extra time. They went on to win 5-2 on the night and 6-4 on aggregate. "To go to the Champions League is something beyond imagination," Dambrauskas said. "We have never qualified for the Conference League, we have never qualified for the Europa League. We have never passed more than two rounds in a row in one competition, and now suddenly we are here." Sabah are based in the town of Masazir - 30 miles north of the Azerbaijan capital Baku - with a population of just 19,000. Known as the Owls, Sabah were only formed in 2017 and on Tuesday will celebrate their ninth birthday. Like many small clubs, their Bank Respublika Arena home, with a capacity of less than 9,000, does not meet Uefa regulations. Instead, the club are expected to play their matches at the Olympic Stadium in Baku. Sabah will host Borussia Dortmund, Barcelona and Napoli, and face a trip to Villarreal - as well as the visits to England. "It can be a very hard draw, and it can be a Sabah draw," said Dambrauskas, clearly excited by the prospect. "You dream for this, to play in this competition, to play against those teams. "So now is the time to show that you can handle it, to find a way to compete and we will try to do this. "We have a good team, we have an ambitious team, we have hungry players who are really keen to show themselves." Sabah president Magsud Adigozalov last week was full of praise for Dambrauskas' impact. "His influence goes beyond tactics," Adigozalov told Report. "He has instilled a mindset and winning mentality in the team. "Even in the most difficult moments, the team never abandons its game or fighting spirit, which is the result of the coach's work." Twenty years ago, Dambrauskas looked out over the pitch at Old Trafford during one of his job interviews, dreaming that one day he would stand in one of the dugouts. Now his coaching career will return to where it started. "I lived in England when the battle between Manchester United and Arsenal was the biggest rivalry. Alex Ferguson and Arsene Wenger," Dambrauskas said. "Now I'm going to come back as a coach in the Champions League and hear that anthem. It's really amazing." Watch highlights of every Champions League game from 22:00 on Wednesday on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app. There will also be a Champions League Match of the Day on BBC One on Wednesday, from 22:40 to 00:00.

item.title: The volunteers risking their lives to defuse Indonesia's wildfire 'carbon bombs'
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1kx4lgy4z4o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The volunteers risking their lives to defuse Indonesia's wildfire 'carbon bombs' - Published The sky grows heavy in Borneo, though not with rain. The air, amber-hued and treacle-thick, is smudged under a blanket of smog that has spilled across international borders – to Singapore, Manila, Kuala Lumpur. Down on the ground, smoke steams from the soil. It's like tear gas, says Dwi Sujatmoko. "It hits your nose straight away, your eyes burn – that's more or less what it's like," he says. "People say these fires are extraordinary because of the flames and the smoke. And they're right." The 35-year-old volunteer firefighter has spent more than a month enveloped in this haze, breathing toxic millennia-old microparticles of carbon as he toils against a seemingly inextinguishable fire front. Using hand tools, carts and portable fire pumps, he and thousands of other volunteer firefighters – many of them indigenous Dayak or Banjar people – are up against an inferno that has carbonised some 200,000 hectares of forest and farmland across Indonesian Borneo since early July. Underground and out of sight, giant subterranean peat fires continue to smoulder, choking the air with poisonous fumes. "Once a fire becomes uncontrolled, it harms many people. Not just humans, but also animals and plants," Sujatmoko says. "If underground fire spreads and can no longer be controlled, the losses are enormous." Indonesia is in the throes of a wildfire catastrophe. Amid a so-called "Super El Niño" that has supercharged local drought conditions, thousands of active fire hotspots are spreading and multiplying across the country, fuelling a transnational haze crisis that is the region's worst in more than a decade. But what makes Borneo's fires particularly worrying is the fact that they are burning through one of the world's largest tropical peatland ecosystems. This 4.5-million-hectare swathe of forest and swamp, under normal conditions, serves as a valuable reservoir for ancient carbon. When these peatlands catch fire, they risk releasing millions of tonnes of carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and methane into the atmosphere – a "pulse" of greenhouse gas emissions that has earned them the sobriquet of "carbon bomb". "Peatlands are incredibly effective carbon stores because their waterlogged conditions slow decomposition, allowing carbon to accumulate underground for thousands of years," explains Dr Nisa Novita, a peatland researcher at Indonesian conservation NGO Yayasan Konservasi Alam Nusantara (YKAN). "But this also means they can become a 'carbon bomb' when they are drained or burned, because that carbon can be rapidly released into the atmosphere. "Tropical peatlands in Indonesia are among the world's most effective natural carbon stores. The deeper the peat, the greater the carbon stock – and in Kalimantan, we have found peat deposits that can exceed 20 metres in depth." A peatland that deep has been known to harbour more than 6,000 tonnes of carbon – roughly equivalent to the annual CO₂ emissions of 4,800 cars – per hectare. And when it burns, says Dr Nisa, that fossilised carbon can be released into the atmosphere "very rapidly". The toxic cloud Thousands of people across South East Asia are now feeling the effects of those emissions in their eyes, chests and throats. Across Indonesia as well as Brunei, Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines, air pollution indices have soared to "unhealthy" extremes - almost 75 times the World Health Organization's recommended level, in some cases – and hospital admissions have surged. Between July and August, Indonesia's Health Ministry recorded over 50,000 cases of respiratory infections linked to land and forest fires. More than 12,000 of them were children under the age of five. "Everybody who's living within that pollution cloud is breathing in the products of those smouldering peat fires," says Susan Page, a professor at the University of Leicester's school of geology and the environment, who's been researching peatlands in Asia for three decades. "They're breathing in carbon monoxide, which is toxic, and they're breathing in the very finely divided particulate matter... [which] can pass through the alveoli in the lungs into the bloodstream and cause further problems elsewhere in the body, including issues with the heart. "Living in this kind of pollution cloud is extremely unhealthy." Nowhere are these health impacts being felt more acutely than at the coalface of the disaster: the fire front. Here, volunteer firefighters have been risking their lives and lungs to extinguish burning peatlands which are notoriously difficult to put out. Two volunteers in Central Kalimantan have died in recent days, reportedly after their health deteriorated from putting out fires. Cloaked in toxic haze that can burn years off a person's lifespan, volunteers have been digging ponds, canals and borewells through bone-dry peat in a desperate attempt to keep their hoses tapped. Some have been driving pipes into the earth, making ad hoc irrigation systems to combat subterranean fires. Others have been sleeping within a stone's throw of the frontline so they can battle the blazes through the night. "The worst thing here has been the smoke," says Fahrin Ramadhianto, a volunteer firefighter in South Kalimantan's Banjarbaru, one of the worst-hit areas. "The smell is like decaying wood being burned – that's the characteristic smell of peat. And that peat contains decomposed wood and organic material from many different sources." An unnatural imbalance Indonesia's peatland fires are not a new phenomenon. Experts say the crisis is rooted in decades of land-use change, dating back to the Suharto era, when vast areas of rainforest and peatland in Kalimantan were opened for logging, plantations and large-scale development projects. Yet authorities have historically avoided blaming industrial actors for causing large-scale fires. Instead, the same indigenous communities who are now engaged in firefighting operations across the island have often been accused of triggering the blazes, due to traditional farming methods that use controlled burns to clear away vegetation. Tono, a representative of the Dayak Kanayatn people of West Kalimantan, told the BBC that Dayak communities are frequently used as scapegoats, despite carrying out land clearing with extensive planning, caution and adherence to multi-generational customs. Tono says these communities' traditional practices, known as uma bukit or "hill farming", are rooted in the idea of maintaining balance with nature. But the natural balance is fast unravelling in Kalimantan, the most deforested area in Indonesia. The region lost almost 160,000 hectares of forest area in 2025, more than one-third of the nationwide figure – much of it to make way for plantations and monocrop agriculture. It is these same industrial-scale development projects that have been largely responsible for draining the area's peat swamps, which renders them significantly more fire-prone, Prof Page says. "Peatlands aren't really the ideal place to set up a plantation – but of course, once the more suitable mineral soils had been exhausted it became possible, by using large machinery, to drain the peatlands and create conditions which would be dry enough," she says. "So not only have you got the deforestation, but peatland drainage of course has also greatly increased the fire risk." Page also points out that, whether on fire or not, a drained peatland emits carbon dioxide into the atmosphere "all of the time". "I think that's forgotten," she says. "I think it's important to recognise that when we see the fires, they're like a dramatic example of what is actually going on the whole time in a drained peatland... The fires are just the worst expression of [that]." Now, as these latest fires continue to spiral out of control, Sujatmoko and others face a concatenation of difficulties in the coming days, weeks and months – not least of which is a shortage of water. Fighting peat fires requires saturating the ground so thoroughly that it becomes "like porridge", Sujatmoko explains. Even then there is a high chance the fire will reappear, like a smoking revenant, fed by hidden fuel buried in the invisible depths of the peat swamp. In the face of these persistent reignitions, ongoing drought conditions and toxic smog, fatigue is another concern. "We're definitely tired," says Sujatmoko. "We get exhausted, we miss our families, our children, our wives. But for now, all of us are putting those things aside. We're doing everything we can to help deal with this haze disaster because it's our duty." "We also hope rain comes soon," he adds. "We've spent months away from home... May all the efforts of those on the front lines be a blessing for everyone." Additional reporting by Faisal Irfani from BBC Indonesian.

item.title: India's high-stakes exam system faces a crisis of trust
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy1g7egy9o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
India's high-stakes exam system faces a crisis of trust - Published In 2017, India introduced the National Testing Agency (NTA) to conduct fair, transparent and standardised examinations. Set up under the federal education ministry, it was meant to make exams more efficient, consistent and trustworthy, after years of paper leaks, administrative errors and cheating allegations. Over the next few years, the agency took charge of some of India's largest and most competitive tests, including medical and engineering entrance examinations, university admissions and eligibility tests for teaching and research. But eight years later, the organisation created to restore trust in India's exams is facing a crisis of confidence of its own. In June, more than two million students had to retake a crucial medical entrance examination after the paper was leaked. The fallout triggered weeks of youth-led protests which eventually led to the resignation of the federal education minister. In response, the government appointed a high-level task force led by tech tycoon Nandan Nilekani to recommend reforms and restore confidence in the examination system. For many Indians, however, the announcement prompted a sense of déjà vu. A similar panel was established in 2024 after irregularities in another medical entrance examination sparked widespread unrest. That committee proposed more than 100 reforms, a little over half of which, external have reportedly been fully implemented. The cycle has repeated: an exam goes wrong, students protest, a committee is appointed and reforms are proposed - only for another crisis to expose the same weaknesses. Experts the BBC spoke to say the problems go beyond paper leaks - from NTA's accountability and capacity to exam centralisation, design and whether India's high-stakes testing system needs a rethink. BJ Rao, who was part of the 2024 panel and is now head of SGT University near Delhi, says India should move more decisively towards computer-based examinations to minimise the chances of paper leaks, increase efficiency and reduce human involvement wherever possible. "Digital connectivity has vastly improved across the country, what we need to do is put in resources and focus on upgrading infrastructure and move to computer-based exams," he told the BBC. "We currently have ad hoc centres for conducting exams. We need to replace them with standardised state-controlled online centres." But technology alone will not solve the problem, he says. Rao points to the NTA's reliance on contract staff: just 24 of its 221 employees are permanent, with many from bureaucratic backgrounds, according to the government. "When you have a large portion of people who work on a temporary basis then there is no sense of belonging, and that has an impact on the functions as well. You need people who are well-versed in academia and experienced in conducting such assessments to ensure better management and oversight," he explains. Some experts argue that repeated crises have exposed flaws not only in how exams are conducted, but also in how they are designed. Keshav Aggarwal, an educationist and president of Educators Federation, says the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (Undergraduate) or NEET-UG - whose paper leak triggered this year's protests - could be restructured along the lines of the country's engineering entrance examination, which is computer-based and conducted in two stages. Rather than relying on a single high-stakes test day, the exams could be held across multiple sessions with different sets of questions, he says. "Different stages and days with varying sets of questions" would reduce the risks associated with any one examination and make the system more resilient to disruptions, Aggarwal explains. Experts also question whether an annual exam can work when millions compete for limited university places. India needs a system where students can take important entrance exams more than once a year, as is common in some western countries, said Yamini Aiyar, senior visiting fellow at Brown University. "This would give students another chance if an exam is cancelled or they do not perform well, reducing the risk of losing an entire year," she says. For millions of Indian students, the risk is real. Many spend years preparing and tens of thousands of rupees on private tuition. A leaked, cancelled or delayed exam can suddenly upend months or years of preparation. Pari, 17, experienced that uncertainty first-hand. After taking NEET this year, she had to retake it after the original exam was cancelled following a paper leak. "It was very frustrating. All our preparation had gone to waste, and we had to start all over again," she said. The experience left her angry at repeated exam failures. "The government can form as many panels as it likes. We need a system strong enough to prevent paper leaks from happening again." Mansi Bansal, 23, has a similar story. She spent months preparing for UGC-NET, a qualification for entry-level college teaching jobs. The exam was cancelled after a 2024 paper leak and again this year after the NTA cited errors in three subjects. Bansal took the affected commerce paper and will retest on 9 September. "I put my life on hold all these months, stopping going to the gym, hanging out with friends or even attending family gatherings," she said. "I had planned my entire year but now it has all gone into uncertainty. Can the government promise a leak won't happen again?" Such experiences have fuelled calls from student activists and opposition politicians to scrap the NTA altogether. Educationists argue that scrapping the agency would not solve the underlying problem. The NTA needs deep structural reform to address recurring failures, but abolishing it is not the answer, said M Jagadesh Kumar, former chairman of India's universities regulator. "A single national testing body offers common security standards, technology, candidate services and result procedures. Creating many new agencies could duplicate costs and produce uneven safeguards," he told PTI news agency. Rao agrees. "It is not a case of all bad news. The body has conducted several exams successfully, where we did not hear of any leaks," he said. What is needed, he argues, is a statutory institution staffed by specialists with the academic, technical and operational expertise to run a secure examination system. Yet for some experts, the debate ultimately goes beyond the NTA itself. Aiyar says the bigger issue is not just stopping the next paper leak, but whether a highly centralised testing system can cope with the intense competition for limited educational opportunities. The NTA may be able to make exams more secure, she says. "But it cannot, at least on its own, change a system in which millions of students compete for a limited number of seats and a single exam can shape their future." Some experts say reform must go beyond the NTA itself: India needs an exam system less reliant on one-off, high-stakes tests, gives students multiple chances and can better withstand disruptions. Rao remains optimistic that the task force led by Nilekani will help plug gaps in the existing system. But for many students, another committee offers little reassurance unless it produces changes they can actually see. "I am studying for my university entrance examination next year," said a 16-year-old Grade 12 student. "In my head I am prepared that there might be a leak. But what can we do about it? I will prepare and hope for the best."

item.title: 'He was a lifeline' - Families at a loss after Haitian caregivers let go in US
item.description:

========================================
'He was a lifeline' - Families at a loss after Haitian caregivers let go in US - Published Long Island mother-of-two Linda Mancuso has been "praying on a daily basis" that her disabled son's Haitian caregiver will be able to come back to work. It was "horrifying," she says, when Jean, who had a temporary work permit, was laid off from work at the end of July from his position at a nonprofit supporting individuals with developmental and intellectual disabilities. Her son Michael is a 5ft 10in, nonverbal 23-year-old. "Showering, sleeping, eating, tying his shoes - Michael can't tie his shoes - I mean, there's so much hands-on involvement, and Jean did all of that," she says. Mancuso was a ball of nerves when she finally agreed to send Michael to residential care, at the age of 19, calling it "the hardest thing I've ever had to do". When he met Jean in the adult home, however, she felt a sense of peace. "Certain people just have it," she says of Jean. "He's literally a lifeline." But Michael lost that lifeline weeks ago, when his employer had to lay Jean off along with 18 other Haitians. Their temporary protected status (TPS) - which allows eligible foreign nationals from unsafe countries to work in the US - had expired. The Trump administration first announced in June 2025 that it would be removing the TPS for Haitians, and the ensuing legal battle went all the way to the Supreme Court. But America's top judges ruled in favour of the administration, paving the way for 350,000 Haitians to lose their status at the end of July. The stripping of that status meant that holders can no longer legally work in the US and are at risk of deportation. The healthcare industry, with a robust Haitian workforce, has been hit particularly hard - with legions of employers forced to fire TPS holders who work directly with patients. Trump cancelled TPS amid a wave of measures restricting immigration, a central plank of his successful 2024 election campaign. Immigration was one of the top concerns for voters in that election and, in Long Island, both counties decisively backed Trump. More than a dozen countries have had their TPS terminated in Trump's second term and Haitians make up nearly a third of all TPS recipients affected. The care industry is feeling the effects. Haiti numbers among the top five countries from which immigrants in the direct-care workforce come, says Kezia Scales, vice-president of policy and research at the Paraprofessional Healthcare Institute. The industry was already under-staffed and waitlists for many care services - from home health aides to assisted living - were already long. "We simply do not have enough people in our domestic market, when you exclude immigrants, to fill those jobs," she tells BBC News. National advocacy groups are campaigning for policies that would strengthen the long-term workforce - including ones that "would expand legal pathways for international caregivers". When asked about the impact of TPS termination, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told the BBC that "Temporary Protected Status is exactly that - temporary". "The assertion that the only way we can support the healthcare industry is by allowing unvetted illegal aliens to remain in the country is grossly false and lazy," the spokesperson said. At AHRC Nassau, which employed Jean, CEO Stanfort Perry sounds exasperated and exhausted. The organisation let go of 19 Haitian staff this year and 22 last year, amidst other immigration crackdowns, he says. "It takes us months to recruit one individual to work in this field, train them and prepare them to provide compassionate, caring support to a person with an intellectual and developmental disability," he says. "I'm competing with fast-food restaurants, grocery stores and retail for staff, because they pay more than what we are able to pay," he adds. It's an issue across the country. At Jewish Community Services of South Florida, which lost 18 Haitian TPS holders, the remaining aides are also working overtime. "That is a huge financial strain on a nonprofit like us," says Sarah Katzenstein, the organisation's director of strategic communications and marketing. The loss of TPS caregivers has been especially damaging to seniors served by the Jewish organisation, as many of them are Holocaust survivors, says Katzenstein. "They had relationships with these home care aides for years - some of them for decades," she says, adding that Holocaust survivors especially can have difficulty trusting strangers. "It's a very intimate relationship, so to these clients, the loss of having their Haiti TPS-holding caregivers truly is devastating." Jewish Community Services has been writing to elected officials to advocate for proposed Senate Bill 4814, which would match a bipartisan bill already passed in the House to extend TPS for Haitians. The effort has currently stalled in the Senate, blocked by Republican opposition. Hundreds of Haitians have been deported since the Supreme Court ruling, despite widespread gang violence in the country. White House czar Tom Homan defended the deportations in a recent CNN interview. "The judges made a decision they must go home. And they need to go home... we're just enforcing the law. And we're doing it in a way that the American people voted for." According to polling released last month by AP-NORC, external, support for Trump's overall immigration policy has fallen 10% since the start of his second term but remains relatively strong compared with other issues like the economy. On deportations, about half of US adults surveyed said Trump had gone too far, which is about the same number as the start of the year. A Pew Research survey in June 2025, external, before the TPS provision was withdrawn from Haitians, suggested 39% of Americans supported the ending of TPS but 59% disapproved. Back on Long Island, Mancuso is grieving the loss of a carer who had actually managed to connect with her high-needs son. "That's one of the things that, as a parent, you worry [about]. Does this kid know that there are other people in the world, other than me, that love him? "And I think he sensed that from Jean - that it's not just a job." Her son might not be able to say it, but she knows he misses Jean and doesn't understand why he's no longer there. For Mancuso, her already-high anxiety about her son's well-being is skyrocketing. "With Jean, I had not a care in the world," she says. She's worried not just for her son but also for the other families served by the local non-profit - and, of course, for Jean and TPS holders like him who are living with uncertainty, unsure if or when they will be deported. "I'm hoping against hope that this thing gets resolved," she says. "I care about [Jean] as a human being, he needs a livelihood - and this has been a livelihood for him, and he's good at it, helping my son. "And it's directly impacting my son by his lack of presence here - and I want him back." Related topics - Published29 August - Published25 August

The man at the heart of a lawsuit brought by 9/11 families had extensive links to Saudi government officials and went paintballing with one of al-Qaeda's future leaders, video obtained by the BBC reveals. How might Lindsay Clancy’s case have unfolded in another country? Lindsay Clancy's murder trial has ended in a mistrial after jurors were unable to unanimously decide on a verdict. The US mother was on trial for strangling her three children. In a number of other western countries, there's a specific law on the books to deal with mothers who kill their young children. It's a term known as infanticide – and generally applies to the killing of a baby in the first year of their life. Co-host of the BBC's Global Story podcast Asma Khalid explains how Lindsay Clancy's case might have unfolded differently elsewhere. Listen to the full episode.
